prompt: In some families, young children are cared for during the working day by their grandparents. Others believe that professional nurseries provide a better start. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
When both parents are in full-time work, the care of a pre-school child has to be arranged by someone. Many families turn to grandparents, while others prefer a registered nursery. I think the two settings supply genuinely different things, and that which one is better depends on what a particular child is short of.

The case for grandparents is partly emotional and partly practical. A grandparent already has a relationship with the child, offers a ratio of attention no institution can match, and provides continuity of place and routine that very young children visibly rely on. There is also the question of cost: full-time nursery fees consume a substantial share of an average salary, and for many households family care is not a preference but the only arrangement that leaves working worthwhile. A grandmother who collects a child three afternoons a week is frequently the reason a second income exists at all.

Nurseries, by contrast, offer things a home cannot. Staff are trained to notice developmental delays early, at an age when intervention is most effective. More importantly, a nursery provides other children. Learning to negotiate, to wait and to lose an argument with an equal is difficult to practise with an adult who is willing to give way, and children who arrive at school without that practice are often the ones who struggle first.

My own view is that the second consideration is decisive for most children. Affection can be supplied at either setting and outside working hours in any case, whereas regular contact with a peer group cannot easily be improvised. I would therefore favour nursery care for the year or two before school, without pretending that every family has the means to choose it.
title: Grandparents or nurseries for young children
